title: Admit the Threat You Missed, Then Change Course
documentTitle: Email from Neal Mohan to Jonathan Bellack et al. Re: Yield Management (October 18–19, 2010)
excerptForBlog:
My interpretation of our two-door strategy meant our primary mission was making DFP the best total revenue management solution, across direct and indirect inventory together; and AdX for non-DFPs was an edge case, not the focus. If we want YM / AdX to make sense entirely without DFP, it would mean minimizing YM features in DFP, to avoid confusion or duplicated effort.

Summarizing -- it sounds like the upshot of this strategy is to compete with the yield managers by investing in more publisher-centric features for AdX, plus an expanded services layer. The devil's advocate question I could imagine stakeholders asking is, how is this materially different from what the AdX publisher strategy was before we started talking about the YM challenge back at the strat summit?

I think getting backfill revenue through the combo of DFP and AdX was a fundamental component of our strategy (and one of the reasons why Google bought DCLK in the first place). And in general it is working — just look at the backfill growth rates. But the reality is we missed the YM threat — both on the AdX side as well as the DFP side. And this was a core mission of AdX. So I think we are altering our approach on both AdX as well as DFP and sales/services to get this right.

lessonTitle: Admit the Threat You Missed, Then Change Course
pullQuote: Strategy reviews are worthless if leaders won't say out loud what they got wrong.
situation: In October 2010, Neal Mohan — Google's VP of Display Advertising at the time — sent an internal email to colleagues about Google's 'yield management' strategy. The question on the table: how should Google's ad-serving product (DFP) and its ad exchange (AdX) respond to independent 'yield managers' who were helping publishers squeeze more revenue from their ad inventory? The stakes were real: Google had bought DoubleClick in part to own this exact backfill revenue opportunity.
insight: Mohan does something unusual here. He points to solid backfill growth — 'just look at the backfill growth rates' — and still says plainly: 'we missed the YM threat.' Most leaders hide behind good numbers. Mohan uses them to set up the harder admission. He also names a specific strategic confusion: the 'two-door strategy' (DFP for publishers with direct sales, AdX for everyone else) had left yield management as an afterthought on both sides. The hidden move in this email is a platform strategy correction. Google had framed AdX as an edge case for non-DFP publishers. Yield managers had exploited exactly that gap. Mohan is signaling the edges need to become the core. He also asks the honest devil's advocate question himself — 'how is this materially different from before?' — which forces the team to answer it before a skeptical stakeholder does.
application: When your top-line metrics look fine, run a deliberate 'threat audit' on the parts of your business you've mentally labeled edge cases or secondary. Competitors rarely attack your strength — they fill the gaps you decided not to prioritize. Write down the devil's advocate question your board or biggest customer would ask, then answer it before your next strategy meeting.
